claims.text: Post-synthesis thermal annealing will produce a stable, restructured catalyst surface.
The annealing-induced surface restructuring will enhance CO oxidation activity.
The annealing-induced surface restructuring will improve resistance to H2O and NO poisoning.
The annealing-induced surface restructuring will improve long-term catalyst durability under low-temperature, transient exhaust conditions.
The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy containing minimal platinum-group-metal content.
The initial catalyst has not received post-synthesis thermal annealing.
Annealing will reorganize the catalyst surface and optimize active-site dispersion.
Annealing may moderate aggregation of Pt sites within a high-entropy-oxide matrix.
Annealing-induced restructuring stabilizes active Pt sites and their interaction with the multi-principal-element matrix.
Stabilization of Pt sites and matrix interactions lowers the CO oxidation onset temperature.
Stabilization of Pt sites and matrix interactions improves poison resistance and mitigates degradation over time.
Relative to the unannealed catalyst, the annealed catalyst will have lower light-off temperatures for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Relative to the unannealed catalyst, the annealed catalyst will maintain higher activity in exhaust containing H2O and NO.
Relative to the unannealed catalyst, the annealed catalyst will retain activity better during accelerated real-driving-emission aging.
The proposed benefits are expected during transient operation below 150 °C in the presence of H2O and NO.
An inadequately optimized annealing temperature may cause excessive sintering or loss of active-site dispersion and thereby reduce activity.

contradictions.description: The starting material is described as an alloy catalyst, whereas the proposed mediator places Pt sites within a high-entropy-oxide matrix. No oxidation step, oxide formation, or alloy/oxide composite structure is specified to reconcile these material identities.
